summary: Proposes the Address plus Port approach to the IPv4 address shortage, in which several hosts share one IPv4 address by each being given a distinct range of port numbers. This avoids giving every host a unique global IPv4 address. It is Experimental.

eli5.summary: One building address can serve many people if each gets their own mailbox number. A+P gives each customer one shared address plus a private range of port numbers.

questions: what is a+p address plus port
how does a+p differ from carrier grade nat
what is a port range router
how does stateless a+p mapping work
subtitle: Share one IPv4 address among many customers by giving each a private slice of the port numbers.

tldr.problem: Providers are running out of public IPv4 addresses and cannot give every customer a unique one, but carrier-grade NATs in the core break end-to-end connectivity and trap users behind fixed rules.
tldr.mechanism: A+P treats some port number bits as an extension of the IPv4 address. Several customers share one address and each gets its own range of ports, with tunnels carrying their packets between the customer device and a Port-Range Router.
tldr.outcome: Customers keep control of translation and some ports need none, while the provider logs only port range allocations. The RFC is Experimental, not a Standards Track specification.

today: RFC 6346 is an Experimental document published in August 2011, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, not as an Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Address Shortage and Carrier Grade NATs
sections.content:
The IANA pool of free IPv4 addresses is running out, and IPv6 is not yet deployed widely enough to replace IPv4. Many large ISPs have so many customers that they cannot give each one a unique public IPv4 address, so some address sharing, in the mold of NAT, is described as inevitable.

The RFC argues against putting Carrier Grade NATs (CGNs) in the core. With a CGN the user is trapped behind application policies they cannot change, and new applications need matching Application Level Gateways on the CGN. A CGN also forces a trade-off between how much session state it keeps and where it sits, and it can become a single point of failure. Intra-domain paths between two nodes behind CGNs may be longer than needed.

The goal is for any translation to happen as close to the edge as possible, with the end user in control.
sections.eli5: When there are not enough street addresses, the post office could sort everything in one big room where you have no say. A+P would rather let each home do its own sorting.

sections.title: Extending the Address with Port Bits
sections.content:
If applications use fewer than 16 bits of port number, the leftover bits can be treated as part of the address. In the RFC's words, between 1 and 65536 customers could share one IPv4 address, each with a fixed or dynamic range of 1 to 65536 ports. This is called extended addressing or A+P (Address plus Port).

The main advantage is that A+P preserves the end-to-end paradigm by not requiring translation, at least for some ports.

The design lists seven constraints: end-to-end under customer control, backward compatibility, a scalable and minimal-state core, a choice between efficiency and complexity, avoiding double NAT, legal traceability from address and port to a customer, and encouraging IPv6 deployment.
sections.eli5: A house number alone is not enough for a big building, so you add an apartment number. A+P uses part of the port number as that apartment number.

sections.title: Three Functions: Tunnel, NAT and Signaling
sections.content:
The architecture splits into three independent functions. Encaps/decaps carries port-restricted A+P packets through legacy devices in a tunnel; a device doing this is a Port-Range Router (PRR). The NAT function serves legacy hosts that assume they own a full address. Signaling tells devices which ports pass untranslated and what happens to the rest.

Two or more devices linked by tunnels form an A+P subsystem. Each is assigned one external address and a range of ports, so packets can reach the public realm without translation. A gateway can delegate part of its port range to another authenticated gateway. In the RFC's example, gateway A holds 192.0.2.1 with ports 0-65535 and delegates ports 2560-3071 to gateway B.

On inbound traffic, A looks at the destination port. If it falls in B's delegated range, A tunnels the packet to B. If it belongs to the co-located large-scale NAT (LSN), the LSN handles it. Otherwise A discards the packet. If the NAT is controlled by the customer it is called an LSN, and if the customer cannot control it, a CGN.
sections.eli5: Think of a mail room that looks at the apartment number on each letter. It sends the letter down the right hallway, hands it to a helper, or throws it away if no one lives there.

sections.title: Signaling and Port Range Allocation
sections.content:
Gateways need to share a set of public IPv4 addresses, a starting port and the number of delegated ports for each address, a lifetime, the tunneling technology and tunnel endpoint addresses, whether the gateway provides NAT, and a device identifier with some authentication. The RFC expects protocols such as PCP, or DHCP and IPCP options, to carry this. Whether NAT is available MUST be communicated in signaling.

Allocating a fixed number of ports to everyone either exhausts heavy users or wastes ports. So the RFC describes dynamic allocation of extra port ranges after an initial static one, preferring the same IP address. The ISP sets the initial size and a maximum number of allocations. A first suggestion is 128 ports initially, then ranges of 128 ports up to 511 more allocations, and one additional allocation per minute would slow a port request storm. A+P-aware applications may ask for a single port, such as a VoIP client.
sections.eli5: Each family first gets a small set of mailboxes. If they need more, they can ask for another set, but not too fast, so nobody hogs them all.

sections.title: Stateless Mapping and Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
The Stateless A+P Mapping (SMAP) function encapsulates IPv4 packets in IPv6. It builds IPv6 addresses from the IPv4 address and port using IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses (RFC 6052) and a provisioned IPv6 prefix. One way to learn the prefix is the well-known default 64:ff9b::/96. In stateless mode no per-flow state is needed, which helps migration towards IPv6-only networks. Binding table mode instead assigns a normal IPv6 prefix and uses a table to match shared address and port range to an IPv6 address, and it supports dynamic port allocation.

In the worked example, a host at 198.51.100.2 sends from TCP port 8000 to 203.0.113.1 port 80. The CPE translates the source to 192.0.2.3 port 100, encapsulates the packet in IPv6 from 2001:db8::2 to the PRR at 2001:db8::1, and the PRR decapsulates and forwards it. Packets with no matching port rule go to the LSN, which MUST NOT use the delegated space.

ICMP echo identifiers are treated like port numbers, and pings from the public side to an A+P device are not supported. Fragments are reassembled to read the destination port, and Path MTU Discovery is recommended.
sections.eli5: The router writes a new return address on the envelope, wraps it in a bigger envelope for the trip across the provider, and unwraps it at the other end.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Customers sharing an address cannot both run a service on the same port, such as port 80, and applications that need well-known ports do not work in A+P unless they adapt. A provider could charge more for the well-known range 0..1024. A+P also shares the IPsec trouble of any NAT that rewrites ports, and the issues in RFC 6269. Experiments reported by France Telecom found most tested applications unaffected, with problems for BitTorrent.

On security, the RFC says LSNs and CGNs make tracing criminals hard, because every connection mapping must be logged and stored, which also worries privacy advocates. With A+P, only the allocation of a port range to a customer must be logged, which happens rarely. If NAT sits on the customer premises, no logging is needed, as with today's NAT boxes. The RFC concludes that A+P is no worse than today and considerably better than CGNs.
sections.eli5: Two families in one building cannot both claim mailbox number 80. And it is easier to remember who got which block of mailboxes than to write down every single letter.
